channel.title: Signal Weekly
channel.description: The week's AI research across LLMs, vision, agents, on-device inference, small models and infrastructure, explained in plain language. By Yathish Reddy.

item.title: Issue 02: Putting work in the right place
item.dc:creator: Yathish Reddy
item.description:
This week's theme is putting work in the right place: prompt reading and answer writing on separate hardware or in separate number formats, cached prompts reused on phone chips, and context that the model edits itself. Google, Anthropic and OpenAI also shipped new frontier, mid-size and agent products.

18 picks across 6 columns. Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
item.content:encoded:
This week's theme is putting work in the right place: prompt reading and answer writing on separate hardware or in separate number formats, cached prompts reused on phone chips, and context that the model edits itself. Google, Anthropic and OpenAI also shipped new frontier, mid-size and agent products.

Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
Each pick below links to its card with the key figure, results table and technical deep dive.

LLMs & language models

Google answered GPT-6 and Opus 5.5 with Gemini 4 Argon, Anthropic's mid-size model caught up with its flagship, and a new paper lets models rewrite their own context.

Gemini 4 Argon takes the lead on long-context and agent benchmarks

Google DeepMind · 30 Sep · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: Google's first Gemini 4 model leads most of its reported benchmarks and allows 1M output tokens, but access is limited at launch.

84.2% GraphWalks, 256K to 1M tokens

Why it matters: Leadership at the frontier changed hands again within ten days of GPT-6 and Claude Opus 5.5, and the introductory price undercuts both.

Read with care: All comparisons come from Google's own table; Argon trails rivals on several coding and science benchmarks, and most people cannot use it yet.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Claude Sonnet 5.5 nearly matches Opus 5.5 at half the price

Anthropic · 28 Sep · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: Anthropic's mid-size model now scores within a few points of its flagship on knowledge-work benchmarks. The price is unchanged, and Anthropic reports output more than 30% faster.

70.6% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Opus 5.5: 66.4%)

Why it matters: Much of the work that needed a flagship model a month ago can now run on a model that costs half as much per token.

Read with care: All scores are Anthropic's own. Opus 5.5 remains well ahead on harder coding sets such as FrontierCode, and the efficiency figures come from selected early testers.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Context Language Models: letting the model edit its own memory

University of Washington · Meta Superintelligence Labs · 29 Sep · paper · code

TL;DR: The model's live context is stored as a file that the model can rewrite freely, which beats fixed summarisation on long tasks and uses less compute.

+11.4% relative accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus, with 21.5% fewer FLOPs

Why it matters: It turns context management from a hand-written rule in the harness into something the model can learn, which matters most for agents that run for hours.

Read with care: Editable context opens new attack surfaces, such as injected instructions that persist across turns. The cache method that saves compute is approximate, and some results come from single runs.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Vision models

No major vision model shipped this week, but three papers changed what counts as hard: better captions, looped layers and an honest map of where general models still fail.

Physis-Lang: better physics in video models by writing better captions

NVIDIA · MIT · University of Oxford · 30 Sep · paper

TL;DR: Rewriting training captions to spell out cause, physical law and effect lifted NVIDIA's open Cosmos3-Nano past Veo 3.1 on three of four physics benchmarks.

71.04 PhyGenBench score, versus 65.63 for Veo 3.1

Why it matters: It shows that an open 16B world model can match or beat a leading closed model on physical plausibility through data and caption work alone, without a physics engine or new architecture.

Read with care: All scores are the authors'. Two benchmarks were re-scored with a GPT-5.5 judge, Veo 3.1 was evaluated by the authors under their own protocol, and the gain on Cosmos3-Edge-4B was small (+3.24 on average).

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Looped-DiT: a small image generator that thinks by repeating its own layers

SenseTime · Tsinghua University · NTU · 30 Sep · paper · code announced

TL;DR: Running the same five transformer blocks four times per denoising step let a 260M-parameter image model beat models up to 6.5 times larger, at lower compute.

71.5 average score, six text-to-image benchmarks (0.26B params)

Why it matters: It adds loop depth as a third way to buy image quality, alongside model size and step count, and in this study it gave more per unit of compute than extra denoising steps.

Read with care: All results are the authors' own, from a small 0.26B pixel-space model built on MiniT2I; it has not been tested at the multi-billion-parameter scale of current leading image models.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Hard vision, easy vision: frontier models tested on 34 computer-vision skills

MBZUAI · Apertix · 28 Sep · independent evaluation

TL;DR: An independent study of six frontier models on 55 benchmarks finds that general models now beat specialists at detection and segmentation but still trail badly at restoration, pathology and geometry.

+10.7 pts GPT-6 Astra over the specialist detector

Why it matters: It is a practical map of which vision tasks can now go to one general API and which still need a dedicated model such as a segmenter, depth estimator or restorer.

Read with care: Generalist outputs had to be converted into each benchmark's format (polygons to masks, for example), and the specialist references differ for each task.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Agentic AI

Agents got their own computers, and research focused on the harness around the model and on recovering from mistakes.

OpenAI gives agents their own computers: Dots and computer use in the Agents API

OpenAI · 29 Sep · vendor launch

TL;DR: At DevDay, OpenAI launched Dots, always-on GPT-6 Astra agents that each run on a dedicated cloud computer, and added computer use to its Agents API.

4,000+ apps a Dot can connect to

Why it matters: Agents now come with a managed, sandboxed computer as standard, so developers do not need to build the loop, the sandbox or the long-session memory themselves.

Read with care: All performance figures come from OpenAI or its customers, and no independent computer-use benchmark results were published with the launch.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

PivotOPD: teaching agents to recover after a pivotal mistake

Princeton University and NVIDIA · 30 Sep · paper

TL;DR: A training method that finds the turn where an agent went wrong and also teaches it what to do next, raising recovery from 8.3% to 72.7%.

72.7% pivotal mistakes recovered (base 8.3%)

Why it matters: Standard training rarely teaches recovery, because the student almost never samples the recovery action on its own; PivotOPD supplies those examples directly.

Read with care: The method relies on the teacher's judgement, and recovery beyond one turn needs an environment that can be replayed exactly, which live websites usually are not.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Raven: composing whole agents, not just prompts

EverMind AI · 27 Sep · paper

TL;DR: Raven treats each model-plus-harness pair as a reusable unit, plans which agents to use as a dependency graph, and automatically evolves each harness around a frozen model.

+13.9 pts BrowseComp+ with an evolved harness

Why it matters: It treats the harness, not just the model, as the thing to compose and improve, which matches how much agent performance currently depends on scaffolding.

Read with care: Several comparisons are internal, reused from earlier publications, or use different budgets and model-based graders, and the authors note that harness evolution can be unstable.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

On-device inference

This week's on-device work targets the wait before the first word, plus a speech front end small enough to run almost anywhere.

Reusing cached prompts on phone NPUs cuts wait time by up to 81%

Shanghai Jiao Tong University · Alibaba · 28 Sep · paper · EuroSys 2027

TL;DR: A system built on ExecuTorch lets Snapdragon NPUs reuse stored attention caches for repeated documents, chats and skill files, even when they are not at the start of the prompt.

40–60% lower time-to-first-token

Why it matters: For on-device agents and document chat, the time before the first word appears is the main delay, and this approach removes most of it on phones that are already on sale.

Read with care: All figures come from the authors' own implementation, and reusing chunks out of order costs up to 4% accuracy on the question-answering tasks.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Whistle: speech to text in a 16.9 MB file

Cactus Compute · 2 Oct · open weights

TL;DR: Cactus released a seven-language speech recogniser that runs on a CPU with no dependencies, gives its first token in 11 ms and is about one-ninth the size of Whisper base.

16.9 MB single file, CPU only

Why it matters: A speech front end small enough for watches, microcontrollers and browsers removes the main reason voice features still go to the cloud.

Read with care: All results are Cactus's own and were published as charts without exact error rates; by Cactus's account Whisper base still does better on TED-LIUM, AMI and the MLS average.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Disaggregated quantisation: one format to read the prompt, another to write the answer

NVIDIA · ISTA · 22 Sep · catch-up · paper

TL;DR: Reading a prompt is limited by arithmetic, while writing tokens is limited by memory. Using NVFP4 for the first and 2-bit weights for the second improves both speed and accuracy.

1.78× faster first token in llama.cpp at 8K context

Why it matters: It offers a way to repair existing community 1- and 2-bit GGUF checkpoints by adding a trained prefiller, without retraining the decoder.

Read with care: Published just before the window; tests cover single-turn, batch-one use only, and the separate prefill weights take extra storage unless they are streamed from SSD.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

SLMs under 1B parameters

Sub-1B models gained steady speed on long inputs, new phone actions, and a way to learn facts and tool calling from synthetic text alone.

IronLLM-0.6B: a 654M model built for robots and car cockpits

Xpeng (Robotics Foundation Model Team) · 29 Sep · paper

TL;DR: Xpeng's 654M-parameter instruct model mixes linear and full attention, keeps decoding at 377 tokens per second at 32K context, and scores 49.4 on BFCL v3.

654M parameters; 327 MB at 4 bits

Why it matters: For a robot or car assistant, steady speed on long inputs and short answers matter more than peak benchmark scores, and this model is designed for exactly that.

Read with care: All results are the authors' own, the speed tests ran on a desktop GPU (RTX 4090) rather than an in-car chip, and the paper does not say whether the weights will be released.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Baguettotron: sub-1B models trained only on synthetic text

PleIAs and academic partners · 29 Sep · paper · Apache 2.0 weights announced

TL;DR: PleIAs trained 56M, 321M and 594M models on SYNTH, a synthetic corpus generated from Wikipedia. The 594M model states facts more precisely than Qwen3-0.6B, which was trained on about 228× more tokens.

41.7% factual macro score, 594M model (Qwen3-0.6B: 31.6%)

Why it matters: It suggests that a small model can be given instruction following, citation-style RAG answers and tool calling from a curated seed corpus, without web-scale data.

Read with care: Knowledge is limited to the seed articles, the helper models were supervised by Gemini 2.5 Pro, most results come from single runs, and the full weights are promised for the camera-ready version.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Teaching FunctionGemma 270M fifteen phone actions

UGrowAI · 21 Sep · catch-up · paper · open dataset and models

TL;DR: With about 9,500 synthetic conversations and two epochs of fine-tuning, Google's 270M function-calling model went from 29.3% to 76.5% end-to-end accuracy on everyday Android actions.

29.3% → 76.5% end-to-end accuracy, 15 phone actions

Why it matters: It shows that a sub-1B tool caller can be extended to new on-device actions with a small synthetic dataset and a single GPU, while keeping private requests on the phone.

Read with care: Published 21 Sep, just before the window. The model trained only on the new actions scores 60.2% on Google's original set versus 90.3% for Google's specialist, and the combined model recovers to 82.3%, still 8 points short.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AI infrastructure

Putting work in the right place: prefill and decode on separate GPUs, experts kept still while tokens move, and near-peak kernels on non-NVIDIA chips.

vLLM splits serving into prefill, decode and a CPU render tier

vLLM project · IBM Research · 29 Sep · open source guide

TL;DR: A vLLM guide shows how running prompt processing and token generation on separate GPUs keeps tail latency steady, and moves tokenisation onto cheap CPU servers.

2.4× goodput, Qwen3-235B on 8× MI300X

Why it matters: It turns a research idea into documented, upstream vLLM configuration, with clear rules for when splitting helps and when it does not.

Read with care: Splitting only pays off when the key-value cache moves quickly: on the authors' PCIe test machine a 470 MB cache took about 1.3 seconds to transfer, and the guide recommends staying on one GPU when time to first token is the binding constraint.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Olmo-core 3: open training code for trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models

Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) · 1 Oct · open source

TL;DR: Ai2 rebuilt its open training stack around expert parallelism instead of FSDP, reporting 2.7× more tokens per GPU on a 47B mixture-of-experts model.

2.7× training throughput, 47B MoE on 8× B300

Why it matters: It is one of the few fully open codebases shown training mixture-of-experts models at the trillion-parameter scale used by frontier labs.

Read with care: Throughput figures are Ai2's own, measured on its own models, and the post offers no head-to-head comparison with established stacks such as Megatron-Core.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

DeepGEMM-Ascend: DeepSeek's matrix kernels reach 98 to 99.8% of peak on Huawei chips

DeepSeek · Huawei · 30 Sep · MIT licence

TL;DR: DeepSeek ported its matrix-multiplication library to Huawei's Ascend 950, reporting near-peak speed in BF16, FP8 and FP4, alongside Ascend versions of its communication and compiler tools.

99.8% of BF16 hardware peak, Ascend 950DT

Why it matters: Software, not raw silicon, has been the main barrier to using non-NVIDIA accelerators, and a leading open-model lab publishing near-peak kernels narrows that gap.

Read with care: Results come from DeepSeek on one hardware and toolkit combination (Ascend 950DT, CANN 9.2) and do not cover other configurations.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Open the full issue · All issues

item.title: Issue 01: Same answers for fewer tokens
item.dc:creator: Yathish Reddy
item.description:
This week's theme is efficiency: the same answers for fewer tokens, large models compressed onto laptops, and agents that improve their own harnesses without overfitting.

18 picks across 6 columns. Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
item.content:encoded:
This week's theme is efficiency: the same answers for fewer tokens, large models compressed onto laptops, and agents that improve their own harnesses without overfitting.

Read the full interactive issue on yathishreddy.github.io →
Each pick below links to its card with the key figure, results table and technical deep dive.

LLMs & language models

Cheaper frontier tiers, and a model trained to reason in fewer tokens.

GPT-6 Sol and Luna halve prices below the flagship

OpenAI · 22 Sep · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: OpenAI's two smaller GPT-6 models cost half as much as their predecessors; Luna is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens.

$0.10 Luna, per million input tokens

Why it matters: A frontier lab's small model now costs about the same as the cheapest open models, which changes the build-versus-buy calculation for high-volume tasks such as classification and extraction.

Read with care: All benchmark results are OpenAI's own; competitor scores were taken from public reports rather than re-run.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Ember-1: the same model, trained to reason in fewer tokens

Fireworks AI · 23 Sep · research preview

TL;DR: Fireworks post-trained Kimi K3 to write shorter reasoning chains, cutting total tokens per task by 39% in a live A/B test with no loss in score.

−39% tokens per task, live A/B test

Why it matters: For agents, the cost per completed task matters more than the price per token, and Ember-1 reduces it by changing only one thing: how much the model writes.

Read with care: All figures are from Fireworks. Ember-1 scores lower on two of the five benchmarks, and serverless access is guaranteed for only two weeks.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Claude Opus 5.5 leads several agentic benchmarks at a lower price

Anthropic · 22 Sep · vendor benchmarks

TL;DR: Anthropic's new model costs 20% less per token than Opus 5 and leads its own comparisons on terminal and coding tasks.

$4 / $20 per million input / output tokens

Why it matters: Model pricing now depends on effort level and caching as much as on the headline rate, so comparisons should be made on cost per task.

Read with care: All benchmarks are Anthropic's own, and the 40% figure compares two different default effort levels.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Vision models

World models that remember a 3D scene, and vision-language models that learn by interacting.

WorldCrafter: a video world model that remembers the scene

Tencent ARC Lab · 21 Sep · open code

TL;DR: A memory queried by camera position keeps a generated scene consistent when the camera returns to a place it has already seen.

−50% revisit inconsistency vs Lyra 2.0

Why it matters: Consistent world models are the foundation for generated game environments, robot simulators and VR scenes.

Read with care: Results are from the authors. The fast variant is more consistent but less accurate in camera control.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

GAE: a latent space that already understands 3D

Tencent ARC Lab · 21 Sep · controlled test

TL;DR: Replacing only the generator's latent space with one built from a 3D perception model cuts video error by up to 23% and halves camera-path error.

−23.1% FVD on DL3DV (lower is better)

Why it matters: It suggests that 3D consistency depends on the representation, not only on model size, and offers one shared interface for perception and generation.

Read with care: Gains are measured against the authors' own baseline. The comparison is controlled but not yet head-to-head with other systems.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Spatial-Interactor: teaching vision-language models through interaction

Zhejiang University · 19 Sep · curriculum

TL;DR: Training on before–action–after sequences, rather than still images, teaches VLMs to track how a scene changes as objects and the camera move.

107,518 interaction QA pairs in LSI-108K

Why it matters: Robots and AR assistants need a mental map that updates as things move, which static-image training does not provide.

Read with care: The authors report consistent gains across several VLMs; the per-benchmark numbers were not verified for this issue.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Agentic AI

Self-improving harnesses, faster agent memory and a training recipe for coding agents.

RRSI: self-improving agent harnesses that generalise

Google and university partners · 21 Sep · most upvoted

TL;DR: Regularising how an agent edits its own prompts and tools trades a small in-domain gain for better results on unseen benchmarks, with fewer tokens.

+4.7 pts JobBench, unseen during evolution

Why it matters: Self-improving agents are now practical, and this work shows that their generalisation can be measured and improved.

Read with care: RRSI gains less than unregularised search on the tasks it evolved on; its advantage appears on unseen tasks.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Jev-Mem: a fast controller for agent memory

Academic (3 authors) · 21 Sep · efficiency

TL;DR: A lightweight controller handles routine memory decisions and leaves the LLM only for reasoning: memory builds 6.6× faster and queries return in 0.93 s.

158 s to build memory (next best 1,044 s)

Why it matters: Memory is where long-running agents become slow and expensive, and removing the LLM from routine lookups is a reusable design pattern.

Read with care: These are early results from a small team on one main benchmark.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Specialise, then merge: training multi-skill coding agents

Alibaba · 20 Sep · no external teacher

TL;DR: Training one agent on every kind of coding task makes some skills regress. Alibaba trains category experts and distils them into one model, improving both benchmarks.

59.0% SWE-bench Multilingual (base 56.2%)

Why it matters: Specialise-then-consolidate is a recipe any multi-skill agent can use, and it needs no external teacher model.

Read with care: Gains are moderate, and all numbers come from the authors' own setup.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

On-device inference

Draft models, GGUF in PyTorch, and ternary weights.

DSpark: a small drafter makes a vision model up to 3× faster

Liquid AI · 24 Sep · output unchanged

TL;DR: A 280M-parameter draft model proposes tokens that Liquid AI's 3B vision-language model verifies in one pass, speeding decoding up to 3.13× on a Mac with identical output.

3.13× decode speed-up on Apple silicon

Why it matters: The drafter is small, which makes it one of the cheapest speed-ups available on device, and it already runs in llama.cpp, MLX-VLM and SGLang.

Read with care: End-to-end gains are well below decode gains because image encoding is slow on edge chips.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Transformers now runs llama.cpp GGUF files directly

Hugging Face · 22 Sep · Apple silicon first

TL;DR: Hugging Face Transformers can load 4-bit GGUF checkpoints and generate on Apple silicon using llama.cpp's own kernels, without expanding them to full size.

8.42 → 2.74 GB Qwen3.5-4B, BF16 vs Q4_K_M

Why it matters: Teams shipping quantised models get one Python path to compare a GGUF conversion with the original checkpoint and to test decoding ideas on the exact weights they deploy.

Read with care: Apple GPUs (MPS) only for now; Hugging Face still recommends llama.cpp for production local inference.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Ternary Bonsai 2: a 27B model in 5.9 GB

PrismML · 17 Sep · catch-up · Apache 2.0

TL;DR: Every weight is stored as −1, 0 or +1, making the model 9× smaller than full precision while retaining 98.2% of its benchmark score.

1.76 bits per weight, effective

Why it matters: This is the most direct route to a 27B-class model on a phone or edge device, and it merits benchmarking on real workloads.

Read with care: Released on 17 September, just before this issue's window. The largest gaps are on knowledge and vision tasks.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

SLMs under 1B parameters

Models under one billion parameters doing one job well. Few sub-1B models were released this week, so two cards are recent references, marked with their dates.

S1-mini: a 0.6B model that cleans up dictated text

Superwhisper · Sep · new on HF · Apache 2.0

TL;DR: A Qwen3-0.6B fine-tune removes filler words, resolves self-corrections and formats numbers, dates and emails, and is small enough to run beside a speech model on a phone.

94.8% token accuracy, 7,519 test cases

Why it matters: It illustrates the best use of a sub-1B model: one narrow, frequent task inside an on-device pipeline, such as voice input on Android.

Read with care: English only; the accuracy figure comes from the vendor's own test set.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Needle 2: function calling in 45M parameters

Cactus Compute · 13 Aug · reference · Apache 2.0

TL;DR: A model built only to choose the right function and fill in its arguments ships as a 14 MB file and runs on watches and low-cost phones.

14 MB complete model at 2-bit weights

Why it matters: A tool router that fits almost anywhere means a larger model is called only when a request needs real reasoning.

Read with care: Released in August and included as a reference. Comparisons are Cactus's own, and the model handles single calls rather than multi-step plans.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Teaching a 350M model to produce valid JSON with 100 RL steps

Hugging Face · Liquid AI model · 3 Sep · reference · free-tier GPU

TL;DR: GRPO with LoRA on a free Colab GPU nearly doubled LFM2.5-350M's JSON compliance, from 18.0% to 31.9%.

+13.9 pts JSON compliance on IFStruct

Why it matters: It is a cheap, repeatable way to make a sub-1B model reliable at the exact output format a tool expects.

Read with care: A community guide evaluated on one benchmark; absolute scores remain low, and larger models still perform better.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

AI infrastructure

Tokenizer speed, paid speed tiers and the real cost of a reinforcement-learning run.

tokenizers v1: 3 to 30 times faster, identical output

Hugging Face · 21 Sep · exact same output

TL;DR: Hugging Face rewrote its tokenizer library with SIMD splitting and a word cache, so text preprocessing no longer leaves GPUs waiting.

3–30× faster encoding, single thread

Why it matters: A faster tokenizer with unchanged output is a free improvement for serving, long-context ingestion and dataset preparation.

Read with care: The largest gains apply only to tokenizers whose split pattern the new splitter recognises, such as GPT-2, cl100k and o200k.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Paying for speed became a standard price line

Industry trend · 21–24 Sep · pricing

TL;DR: Anthropic, xAI, Alibaba and Xiaomi all launched paid fast tiers this week: the same model at 2 to 10 times the price for higher output speed.

10× price for MiMo UltraSpeed

Why it matters: Latency is now a priced product: interactive traffic can go to fast tiers and background work to batch tiers, which cost half.

Read with care: Measure time-to-first-token and throughput independently before paying the premium.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Xiaomi published the cost of a reinforcement-learning run

Xiaomi · 22 Sep · MIT licence

TL;DR: Six days of reinforcement learning cost about $0.85M for MiMo-V2.6-Flash and $2.62M for Pro, and the environments and framework are open source.

$2.62M 6-day RL run, MiMo-V2.6-Pro

Why it matters: It is a rare real data point for budgeting post-training, and it shows that generating attempts costs as much as updating the model.

Read with care: Excludes pre-training, staff, failed runs and earlier research; no hardware type or hourly rate is given, and nothing is audited.

Open the figure, results and deep dive →

Open the full issue · All issues
